reading.rtitle: The Letter on the Label Means Almost Nothing
paras: In the United States, a size is not a measurement. It is a decision made by the brand. The same woman can be a small in one store, a medium in the store next door, and a small again on a website that sells the same shirt. Nobody is lying to her. There is no law that says what a medium has to be, so every company writes its own size chart, and a lot of those charts are twenty or thirty years old. That is why people who have shopped here for a while stop trusting the letter on the label and start reading the numbers underneath it.

Once you stop trusting the letter, the words in the description do the work. When a website says a garment is snug, it means close to the body: you will get into it, and you will feel it on your shoulders when you raise your arms. When it says baggy, it means the piece was cut much bigger than the body on purpose. Neither word is a warning, and neither one is a mistake. They are choices. If the shoulders are right and the waist is not, take the fitting room seriously and try on a size up before you decide. Sleeves are the part everybody forgets, and sleeves are usually the problem.

Then there is the color, which is where the confusion usually wins. Catalogs almost never write blue or red. They write turquoise, a bright blue-green, like water over pale sand; burgundy, a dark red, the color of red wine; charcoal, a grey so deep that it is nearly black; and mustard, a heavy yellow with brown in it. A salesperson who says the burgundy one is not making your life difficult. He is using the only name the store gave that color. Learn eight of these names and half of the catalog becomes readable. The pattern works the same way: stripes, dots and flowers are described in words, not shown.

The last lines on the tag decide how long the garment lives. Machine washable means the machine is safe. It does not mean hot water is safe. Heat is what makes a dark color fade, and heat is what makes cotton shrink, usually in the dryer rather than in the wash. Turn the piece inside out, wash it cold with similar colors, hang it to dry away from the window, and a black hoodie is still black two years later. Do it the fast way and the same hoodie is grey by March, one size smaller, and nobody at the store is going to take it back.

listenings.text: Good afternoon, shoppers, and thank you for being with us today. Our end-of-season sale is now open on all three floors. On one, coats and jackets are thirty percent off, and that includes every garment on the winter wall. On two, you will find sweaters, hoodies and everything with a pattern at half price. Yes, half. Three is denim, and denim is buy one, get the second at forty percent off. Now, a quick word about the fitting rooms. There is a six-item limit today, the fitting rooms on two are closed for repair, so please use the ones on three, and our associates cannot hold anything at the counter while you keep shopping. And please note, sale items can be returned or exchanged within fourteen days, not thirty, with the tag still attached and the receipt in the bag. Fourteen days. We close at nine tonight. Thank you, and enjoy the sale.

So I ordered a coat online, in the size I always take, and when it came it did not even close. I mean, at all. And I almost sent it straight back, and then I actually read the page, and there it was, a size chart, right under the picture, with the measurements in inches. Chest, waist, sleeve. And it turns out that in that brand my usual size is two inches smaller than in the store I go to at home. Two inches. Nobody tells you that. So now I do this. Before I buy anything, I take a garment I already own, one that fits me properly, I lay it flat on the bed, and I measure it. Chest, waist, sleeve, in inches. And then I compare those numbers to the chart, not to the letter on the label. And honestly, I have stopped guessing, and I have stopped ordering a size up just in case.

Thanks for calling our care line. Here is the recorded answer to the question we get most, which is, why did my sweatshirt come out smaller? Almost always, it is heat. Machine washable means the machine is fine. It does not mean hot water is fine. So, wash cold, thirty degrees or below, turn the garment inside out, and wash it with similar colors, dark with dark. That inside-out step is the one people skip, and it is the one that keeps the color from rubbing off inside the drum. Now, the dryer. Do not tumble dry cotton on high. That is what shrinks it, not the wash, and it is usually a full size. Hang it to dry instead, and away from a window, because strong sun will make a dark color fade just as fast as hot water will. And never bleach a pattern. Bleach does not take out the stain. It takes out the design.
